name: Matra MS11
hook: France's first Grand Prix V12 scored a single podium, yet it was the loudest car on the grid, and its descendants won Le Mans three years in a row.
story:
In 1967, France wanted a Grand Prix engine of its own. The oil company Elf paid for it. The government lent six million francs. A former Simca engineer, Georges Martin, drew a V12.

It arrived at Monaco in May 1968, in a slim blue car called the MS11. Jean-Pierre Beltoise drove it.

It was not a success. It ran hot. It drank fuel. It broke. Matra's other team used a British Cosworth V8, and Jackie Stewart won races with it. The V12 managed one podium all year, second in the rain at Zandvoort. Stewart won that day, so the top two were both Matras.

What people remembered was the noise. Its six exhaust pipes made it the loudest car on the grid.

Matra did not give up. Versions of that V12 won Le Mans three years running, from 1972 to 1974. And in 1977, in Sweden, a Matra V12 in a Ligier carried Jacques Laffite to the first all-French win in world championship history.

Hear one once, fans say, and you never forget it.
description: The MS11 was the Formula One car Matra built in 1968 to carry its own engine, the MS9 V12. The three-litre, 60-degree V12 was designed by Georges Martin and paid for by Elf and a French government loan. It sat in an aluminium monocoque and drove through a Hewland five-speed gearbox. Jean-Pierre Beltoise raced it, and his best result was second at the 1968 Dutch Grand Prix. Matra's Cosworth-powered MS10 outpaced it, but the engine became the root of Matra's Le Mans winners.
